paragraphs.text: Malonyl-CoA decarboxylase (MLYCD) deficiency is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by malonic aciduria, developmental delay, seizures, hypoglycemia, and cardiomyopathy (Wightman et al., 2003). Gao et al. (1999) listed mild mental retardation, seizures, hypotonia, cardiomyopathy, vomiting, hypoglycemia, metabolic acidosis, and malonic aciduria among its features. Sacksteder et al. (1999) described it as a lethal disorder characterized by cardiomyopathy and developmental delay. Malonyl-CoA decarboxylase catalyzes the proton-consuming conversion of malonyl-CoA to acetyl-CoA and CO2 (Sacksteder et al., 1999; Gao et al., 1999).

paragraphs.text: In their patient, Haan et al. (1986) found increased urinary amounts of malonic, methylmalonic, succinic, adipic, glutaric, and suberic acids. Mitochondrial malonyl-CoA decarboxylase activity in extracts of his cultured fibroblasts was 4% of the mean control value. A high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet led to symptomatic hypoglycemia, moderate metabolic acidosis, and urinary excretion of large amounts of the same organic acids and of 3-hydroxybutyrate. On an isocaloric low-fat, high-carbohydrate diet, he excreted only relatively small quantities of malonic, methylmalonic, and succinic acids. Acute fat and lysine loads increased urinary malonic acid excretion without affecting excretion of the other organic acids.

paragraphs.text: FitzPatrick et al. (1999) studied 2 previously reported patients with MCD deficiency from consanguineous Scottish families. By RT-PCR analysis of fibroblast RNA from one patient, they identified a homozygous nonsense mutation in the MCD (MLYCD) gene (S148X) that created a premature stop codon in the N-terminal half of the protein. In the second patient, they identified a homozygous intronic mutation (IVS4-14A-G) that created a novel splice acceptor site, causing a 13-bp insertion in the mature RNA, a frameshift, and predicted truncation of the protein. Each mutation segregated appropriately within the family and was absent from 100 normal unrelated individuals.

paragraphs.text: Wightman et al. (2003) sequenced the genomic MLYCD gene in 9 unrelated patients with MLYCD deficiency and identified 16 of the 18 pathogenic alleles. They recorded the variants in a newly created Human MLYCD Allelic Variant Database. Western blot analysis of fibroblast cell lines from 8 of their patients and 2 previously reported patients with homozygous MLYCD mutations showed that the 66-kDa MLYCD band was absent in 6 patients and substantially reduced in 3. One patient had increased protein levels, with a prominent smeary band at 68 to 83 kDa. The mutations included an extreme N-terminal mutation (G3D), whose mutant protein mislocalized to the plasma membrane on immunocytochemistry; a mutation (M40T) that ablates the second of the putative mitochondrial and peroxisomal initiating codons; and a 25-base deletion between the putative mitochondrial (M1) and peroxisomal (M40) initiating codons. The protein from the last 2 mutants showed punctate perinuclear staining.

paragraphs.text: Sacksteder et al. (1999) found that recombinant MCD protein had high intrinsic malonyl-CoA decarboxylase activity and carried a canonical type-1 peroxisomal targeting signal (serine-lysine-leucine at the C terminus). Subcellular fractionation showed that MCD is located in both the cytoplasm and peroxisomes. They proposed that cytoplasmic MCD regulates the amount of cytoplasmic malonyl-CoA and, through it, mitochondrial fatty acid uptake and oxidation. They noted that MCD mRNA is most abundant in cardiac and skeletal muscle and that patients have phenotypes reminiscent of mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation disorders. They also suggested that peroxisomal MCD may degrade intraperoxisomal malonyl-CoA produced by beta-oxidation of odd chain-length dicarboxylic fatty acids.

paragraphs.text: Wightman et al. (2003) found apparent intracellular mislocalization of MLYCD in patient cell lines that still expressed the protein. None of the 3 mislocalizing mutations was predicted to alter catalytic function, so the authors concluded that correct subcellular localization of MLYCD is likely critical for normal function. They suggested that a novel targeting signal may reside in a conserved 4-amino acid N-terminal motif.
